extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, literary critics, and theatre managers/readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical principles for judging and producing poetry, translation, and dramatic repertory — covering language, versification, subject-choice, translation fidelity, theatrical programming, and qualifications for theatre management. Extracted from literary-critical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration / unity of impression in language
rubrics_metrics.description: The German power of 'condensing meaning' consists in the unity and simultaneousness with which an impression is conveyed; it makes the language more picturesque and depicts images better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not merely speed of conveying impression but the ability to present a single unified impression; comparisons: German and Greek show this power. Example: compound verbs and prefixation in German contribute to this pictorial concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of native prefixed particles vs Latin derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixed particles that convey no separate meaning to the English reader (Latin derivatives) cannot act on the mind with the same force or liveliness as genuine native prefixes/compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of Latin-derived compounds which may weaken vividness; prefer native formations when aiming for forceful, picturesque diction (Milton both used and abused Latin derivatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and prolonged composition practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should be planned thoroughly (Klopstock finished his plan before reading Milton) and composition often proceeds only in favorable moments; long projects may consume many years while actual composition occupies comparatively little time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a well-formed plan and episodic productive moments rather than constant forced output; publishing in parts over time is acceptable; patience in finishing a long poem is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure/plan of odes and lyrical pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear plan of the ode is a mark of excellence — Klopstock valued the plan of his odes and accused modern lyrical writers of gross deficiency in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure lyric compositions have cohesive structural design rather than being loose assemblages of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject and poetic ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should aim to raise readers to their own level rather than descend to readers' level; relying on appetites (e.g., erotic gratification) to sustain long poems is a cheap way of pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects like the passion of love can be suitable, but avoid sustaining long works by pandering to base appetites; the great poet elevates the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of cheap sentimentality (easy tear‑jerking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to excite tears is easy and often used by meanest writers; true poetic merit lies beyond merely deluging an audience with sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of devices that provoke mechanical emotion; aim for genuine emotional elevation rather than cheap effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification: sweep and movement over pedantic exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better for the general sweep and movement of a verse to be superior than for final terminations (exact rhymes) to be perfectly exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor inaccuracies in final sounds can be excused if the overall movement and sweep of the verse are superior (Dryden preferred for variety of movement vs Pope's exactness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for language-specific rhyme conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: English does not distinguish masculine and feminine rhymes like French; translators or poets should not rigidly import foreign rhyme distinctions into English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of native prosodic conventions; avoid forcing another language's rhyme rules onto English verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about borrowing idioms from other tongues
rubrics_metrics.description: Enriching a language by borrowing idioms is a dangerous practice; Milton often injured his prose and verse by taking idioms too frequently from other languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer models of 'pure and native English' (prose of Dryden recommended); use borrowed idioms sparingly and with care so as not to dilute native force and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful imitation in translation without sacrificing target-language idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation renders the original with fidelity and imitative harmony so as to suggest the original words, but must respect the spirit and idiom of the target language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Voss: rendered the Greek with fidelity and imitative harmony without 'sacrificing' German idiom to the Greeks; avoid forcing source-language idioms that violate the target language's genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate versification form for language and subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Different languages and their poetic histories admit or resist certain metrical forms (hexameters, blank verse, measured prose); success depends on suitability and craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier German attempts at hexameter had moderate merit; experiment carefully and attend to ease and suitability of versification for the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic writing requires action and clear plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful drama should have sufficient action and a plot that is not inextricable; tediousness arises from lack of action, and extravagance or inextricable plotting undermines dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lessing praised as chaste; Nathan criticized for being tedious (not enough action); Schiller criticized for extravagance and inextricable plots — aim for clarity, adequate action, and proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling as source of poetic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful diction, admirable harmony, and life-like expression in works (e.g., Bürger's ballads) may arise from the poet's own violent feelings and life experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic personal experience and intense feeling can produce vivid, living poetry; craft must shape that material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable appropriation of myth/romance materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Older books and fables of romance can be treated as a kind of common property from which an author is free to take whatever he can make good use of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing from ancient or popular materials is permissible provided the poet makes genuinely good artistic use of them rather than merely copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's duty to render striking passages and manage imperfect joins
rubrics_metrics.description: A translation should capture very striking passages and account for the imperfect joins of a translated work; defects in translation may obscure otherwise striking original passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize where the translator's imperfection affects reception; valuable translations should convey salient beauties and mitigate awkward joins where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for responsible theatre management
rubrics_metrics.description: To restore a theatre (e.g., Drury Lane) to classical renown, the concern should be farmed to a responsible individual possessing rank, fortune, liberal education, critical discernment, delicate tact, disinterestedness, and unsuspected integrity — not a mercenary manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management should be entrusted to persons with social standing and cultural taste who will resist mercenary temptations and champion high repertory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repertory standards for restoring the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration of the British stage requires removing zoological rarities and pernicious barbarisms and reinstating classical dramatists (Shakspeare, Jonson, Otway) and the expurgated comic repertory of Vanbrugh, Congreve, Wycherley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming should favor classical and serious dramatic works over spectacle, imported barbarisms, and low amusements; aim for taste, dignity, and traditional standards of excellence.
